title: Two identical elastic bars colliding (explicit contact)
source: One-dimensional elastic impact of equal bars: contact for 2L/c, interface force ρcAv₀/2, exchange of velocities, no loss of energy; Graff, Wave Motion in Elastic Solids, Dover 1991, §2.1–2.3; Johnson, Impact Strength of Materials, Arnold 1972, §1.6

quantities.quantity: time of the last contact (the bars touch from t = 0) against 2L/c = 0.2
quantities.reason: the penalty springs at the interface delay the release by a few element transit times (about 1% of 2L/c with 200 elements per bar)

quantities.quantity: the largest force across the interface against ρcAv₀/2 = 0.05
quantities.reason: the plateau is ρcAv₀/2 to 0.01%; the peak is the plateau plus the ringing behind the discrete wave front, a few percent

quantities.quantity: velocity of the struck bar's far end after the impact (0: the striker stops)
quantities.reason: the striker stops on average (its kinetic energy is under 0.01% of the start's, see ke); its far end node keeps the ringing of the discrete release front, a few percent of v₀

quantities.quantity: velocity of the struck bar's far end after the impact (v₀ = 0.1)
quantities.reason: the struck bar leaves at v₀ on average; its far end node keeps the ringing of the discrete wave fronts, a few percent

quantities.quantity: kinetic energy after the impact over ½mv₀² (frictionless elastic impact)
quantities.reason: an elastic impact keeps the kinetic energy; the quadratic bulk viscosity at the compression fronts and the vibration left in the bars take a fraction of a percent

quantities.quantity: energy left in the contact after the separation, over ½mv₀² (its drift)
quantities.reason: the penalty springs give back what they took; the trapezoidal work of a spring that engages between increments drifts by far less than 0.1%
